verdict.content_summary: Teknium's technical post-mortem of Hermes Agent (Nous Research's open-source coding agent) autonomously refactoring its own 1.06M-line Python repo: a standing /goal objective fanned out to 1,393 subagents (218 concurrent) across 36 non-overlapping file groups in separate git worktrees, with a three-level delegation tree where the root agent only writes briefs, integrates branches, and runs checks. Workers were steered by an agent-maintained markdown 'skill file' of accumulated procedures and gated by machine-checkable contracts (identical JSON tool schemas, byte-for-byte --help diffs, frozen test-failure baselines, commit-per-verified-step), cutting non-test LOC 34.4% and gateway/run.py from 34,847 to 5,512 lines for ~$25k of remote Claude inference orchestrated by a single local Python process on an i7/64GB desktop. The post is unusually honest about failure modes: an expired auth token killed the run at 50 minutes (recovered via surviving commits and briefs plus a separate handoff-prep session), community review caught cross-plugin breakage the tests missed, and the tokens-per-lookup benchmark (2,218→993) is explicitly caveated as measuring lookup cost, not task performance. Ops lessons fold back into the repo: a shared Pyright server across ~30 worktrees to kill 8.7 GB of duplication, and an automated guardrail flagging removal of public names for review.

grabs.what: Agent-authored markdown skill file that accumulates reusable procedures from daily use and is shared so other instances inherit them
grabs.why: Pure plain-text-first — it's the same medium as their markdown-in/structured-queues-out pipeline. They can port this to their own coding and doc agents today without adopting Hermes: write procedures once, in markdown, where both humans and future agent sessions consume them, versioned alongside the code.

grabs.what: Worktree-per-worker fan-out with a coordinator-only root: non-overlapping file partitions, written briefs per worker, three-level delegation, integration and checks consolidated at the top
grabs.why: Matches 'cheap beats fancy' — the entire orchestrator was one local Python process on a desktop, with inference billed per-token via API, which is exactly their OpenRouter-style BYO-key setup. They already run local coding agents, so this is a directly portable blueprint for parallelizing refactors or doc-processing jobs on hardware they own.

grabs.what: Machine-verifiable completion contracts plus durable-by-construction runs: byte-for-byte --help comparisons, JSON schema identity, frozen failure baselines, commit after each verified step, and crash-resume via surviving commits/briefs and a handoff doc written by a separate session
grabs.why: This is 'prose is for humans, data is for machines' applied to trust: no trusting agent self-reports, only checkable invariants, with every verified step doubling as saved state. They can wire the same gates into their own pipelines so a killed run costs a resume, not a restart.

grabs.what: Hermes Agent itself — open-source, single-process local orchestration, remote inference brought via key
grabs.why: They run local coding agents and route models by key, and Hermes' orchestrator never leaves the machine while inference stays BYO-key — no per-seat subscription, no data locked in someone else's cloud. Even if they don't adopt it wholesale, the /goal standing-objective loop and the orchestrator's brief/integrate/check split are crib-worthy.

finds.name: Effective harnesses for long-running agents (Anthropic Engineering)
finds.what_it_is: Engineering writeup of a file-based harness for multi-session agents: an initializer session writes an init.sh, a claude-progress.txt log, and an initial git commit; every subsequent session makes incremental progress and leaves structured updates so a fresh context window can reconstruct state.
finds.different_angle: Shares the triaged post's crash-recovery mechanism (per-step commits plus a file that carries state across amnesia) but inverts the topology: Anthropic's pattern is a single linear chain of sessions resuming from a progress file, whereas Hermes fanned out a delegation tree with briefs — a useful contrast for deciding when one durable thread beats orchestration.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Directly portable into the user's local agent pipelines: progress-file plus git-commit checkpointing is plain-text, works offline, needs no managed database (fits the SQLite/cheap-beats-fancy ethos), and is exactly the kind of harness mechanism they want to port rather than buy.

finds.name: planning-with-files — crash-proof markdown plans for coding agents
finds.what_it_is: Open-source convention for persistent file-based planning: crash-proof markdown plans re-injected every turn, a progress.md, and a Topic Handoff Pattern (handoffs/*.md alongside progress.md) for long-running operational work; survives /clear and compaction.
finds.different_angle: Same mechanism as the post's recovery-via-surviving-commits-and-briefs, but packaged as a reusable, agent-agnostic markdown convention any local agent can adopt, instead of a bespoke one-run recovery story.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Markdown-first, self-hosted, no accounts or cloud — matches the plain-text-first stack and gives their ingest/agent pipelines a drop-in crash-resume layer built from files they can read and version in git.

finds.name: SKILLS.md: an open agent skills protocol
finds.what_it_is: Proposed open protocol where a single SKILLS.md instruction file (or a reference CLI: atskills get/save/triggers/prompt) turns any agent that can read files and run shell commands into a full skills client; resolved skills are just files on disk, with resolution, cache, and trigger rules specified.
finds.different_angle: Takes the post's agent-maintained markdown skill file and standardizes it into a vendor-neutral protocol with explicit resolution and trigger semantics — the mechanism as spec plus CLI rather than one repo's emergent convention.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Open, single-purpose, no vendor lock-in, BYO-everything: skills as plain files on disk compose with the small-tools philosophy and the multi-model OpenRouter/local setup, and the reference CLI is something to port or fork.

finds.name: ONTO: a token-efficient columnar notation for LLM input
finds.what_it_is: Paper proposing ONTO, a columnar serialization for LLM input: field names declared once per entity, pipe-delimited rows, indentation for hierarchy; 46–51% token reduction vs JSON while staying human-readable and supporting nested data.
finds.different_angle: Attacks the same tokens-per-lookup problem the post benchmarked (2,218→993) at the data-format layer — redesign the serialization so cheap lookups hold by construction — instead of restructuring docs and measuring the delta afterward.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Their pipeline is 'markdown in, structured queues out' and they explicitly want data shaped for machines; ONTO is a concrete, portable format for the structured side of that pipeline, cutting token cost on OpenRouter billing and local context windows alike.

finds.name: Markdown task files as an agent coordination queue
finds.what_it_is: A coordination scheme where each task is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter (id, status, claimed_by, depends_on, priority); agents scan the files to find available or unblocked work — the frontmatter is the entire coordination protocol.
finds.different_angle: Same 'markdown files steer agents' substrate as the post's skill file, but carries work-state (a claimable queue with dependencies) instead of accumulated procedure — the filesystem as a task queue rather than as memory.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: This is literally 'markdown in, structured queues out' applied to agent work: plain files, no server or database beyond the filesystem, composable with their local agents, and a mechanism they can graft onto the existing ingest pipeline.
